user_query: How do LINE and node2vec approach information network embedding, and how do breadth-first search and depth-first search relate to their sampling strategies?
llm_response: LINE and node2vec are both methods for learning low-dimensional embeddings of nodes in a graph, but they do so in different ways. LINE (Large-scale Information Network Embedding) is designed to preserve first-order and second-order proximity in a network: first-order proximity keeps directly connected nodes close in the embedding space, while second-order proximity preserves similarity between nodes that share similar neighborhoods. node2vec, in contrast, learns embeddings by generating biased random walks over the graph and then applying a skip-gram-style objective to predict context nodes from walk sequences. Its sampling strategy is controlled by two parameters that interpolate between breadth-first search (BFS) and depth-first search (DFS): BFS-like walks tend to stay near the starting node and capture local, homophily-oriented neighborhoods, while DFS-like walks explore farther away and capture more structural or role-based similarity. In short, LINE uses explicit proximity-preserving objectives, whereas node2vec uses biased random-walk sampling; BFS corresponds to more local sampling and DFS to more exploratory sampling in node2vec.
llm_confidence_reasoning: This is a standard, well-established description of LINE and node2vec and their BFS/DFS sampling interpretation, so I am highly confident in its factual accuracy.
